lektioner.om: This introduction introduces the philosophy of The Thinking Method for Complete Spanish. It emphasizes active participation through pausing the audio to construct responses rather than relying on memorization or note-taking. Learners are encouraged to think slowly, study in short daily sessions, and engage deeply with the thought processes behind sentence construction.
koncept: Introduction to The Thinking Method
Active participation vs. passive listening
No memorization / no note-taking rule

lektioner.om: Lesson 1 introduces the relationship between English and Spanish via Latin roots, demonstrating that English words ending in -al are generally identical in Spanish. The lesson emphasizes Spanish phonetic pronunciation, vowel clarity, stress on the final syllable for words ending in -al, and builds simple affirmative and negative statements using the verb 'es' and 'no es'.

ord.en: is / it is / he is / she is / you (formal) are

fraser.en: It is normal. / He is normal. / She is normal.
He is liberal. / She is liberal. / It is liberal.
It is not. / He is not. / She is not.

koncept: Latin cognates ending in -al remaining identical in spelling in Spanish
Stress shifts to the final syllable for words ending in consonants other than n or s
Spanish pure vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u) and phonetic consistency
The verb 'es' meaning 'is', 'it is', 'he is', 'she is', and formal 'you are'
Negation by placing 'no' directly before the verb ('no es')
Connecting vocabulary roots to remember new words (dental -> diente; verbal -> verbo)

lektioner.om: This lesson teaches how to convert thousands of Latin-derived English words into Spanish by recognizing word endings like -ant/-ent (becoming -ante/-ente) and -able/-ible. It introduces the adverbial suffix -mente (equivalent to -ly) and explains the Spanish pronunciation of soft 'g' sounds as friction in the throat. The teacher encourages active experimentation with English-Spanish cognates to build a large vocabulary quickly.
koncept: Conversion of English words ending in -ant/-ent to Spanish by adding -e (-ante/-ente)
Forming adverbs by adding the suffix -mente to adjectives (equivalent to English -ly)
Pronunciation shift of English 'soft g / j' sounds into the Spanish aspirated 'j' / 'g' sound (e.g. general, digital)
Cognates ending in -able and -ible with stress falling on the penultimate syllable

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the conversion rule for English words ending in -ion/-ation to Spanish nouns ending in -ión/-ación and verbs ending in -ar. The teacher explains positive and negative language transfer and introduces the verb 'quiero' ('I want') along with attached reflexive object pronouns like in 'prepararme'.

fraser.en: I love you. / I want you.
I want to prepare myself. / I want to get ready.

koncept: Words ending in -ion convert to -ión with final stress in Spanish
Words ending in -ation (-ación) convert to verbs ending in -ar by replacing -ación with -ar
Positive vs. negative language transfer
Direct/reflexive object pronoun 'me' attached to infinitives (prepararme)
Negation by placing 'no' before the verb (no quiero)

lektioner.om: Introduces the emphatic subject pronoun 'yo' and object pronouns 'lo' ('it'/'him') and 'te' attached directly to the end of infinitives. Expands vocabulary building by deriving -ar verbs systematically from English/Spanish -tion/-ción nouns and converting -ence/-ance nouns to -encia/-ancia. Discusses Spanish rolling 'r' pronunciation mechanics and minimal pairs like 'pero' vs 'perro'.

ord.en: to oblige, to make (someone do something)

fraser.en: I want to find out / inform myself.
I don't want to oblige you / make you.
I don't want to provoke you.
I want to save him / save it.

koncept: Subject pronoun 'yo' used mainly for emphasis
Object pronoun 'lo' attached to infinitives for 'it' and 'him'
Object pronoun 'te' attached to infinitives for informal 'you'
Reflexive infinitive: 'informarme' (to inform myself / to find out)
Deriving verbs from -ción nouns via the root (celebración -> celebrar, obligación -> obligar, creación -> crear)
Cognate conversion rule: English '-ence' / '-ance' to Spanish '-encia' / '-ancia'
Pronunciation distinction between single 'r' (tap) and double/initial 'r' (rolled rr) using minimal pairs (pero vs. perro)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the verb 'intentar' (intento) and 'ir' (voy), while practicing combining longer sentences with 'pero'. It covers Spanish pronunciation rules, emphasizing the silent 'h', standard 's' sounds (avoiding the English 'z' sound), and the soft bilabial 'v/b' pronunciation.

fraser.en: I'm trying to imitate it / him.

fraser.es: Quiero cancelarlo pero no quiero cancelarlo ahora.
fraser.en: I want to cancel it, but I don't want to cancel it now.
I want to visit him / it.

koncept: Silent 'h' in Spanish pronunciation
Pronunciation of Spanish 'v' and 'b' (soft bilabial sound vs. plosive)
Breaking down compound words (a + hora = ahora)
Expressing intention and ongoing action with simple present ('intento', 'voy')
Chunking longer complex sentences connected by 'pero' (but)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the crucial grammatical rule of placing the preposition 'a' after verbs of motion (such as 'voy' and 'pasar') before an infinitive verb. It also shows how to pluralize the direct object pronoun 'lo' to 'los' (them) and derives new verbs like 'mostrar' from Latin roots ('demostración'). Students practice distinguishing when to use the connecting 'a' versus stacking infinitives directly after verbs of intention or desire.

fraser.en: I want to show you something.
I am going to confiscate it.
I am going to examine it.
I am going to see them.
I am going to try to see them.
I am going to pass by to visit you.
I am going to pass by to visit you (formal) / him.

fraser.es: Voy a intentar pasar a visitarte.
fraser.en: I am going to try to pass by to visit you.
I want to pass by to show you something.

koncept: Using Latin root conversions to find English/Spanish equivalents (carry on -> continuation -> continuar)
Connecting verbs of movement (motion verbs like 'ir/voy', 'pasar') to subsequent infinitives using the preposition 'a'
Forming the plural direct object pronoun 'los' (them) from 'lo' (him/it)
Attaching object pronouns directly to the end of infinitives (e.g., continuarlo, mostrarte, verlos, visitarte)
Contrasting motion verbs requiring 'a' with non-motion verbs like 'querer' and 'intentar' which take infinitives directly without 'a'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces feminine object pronouns ('la', 'las') alongside masculine forms ('lo', 'los') and discusses grammatical gender. It explores the shared verb ending for he/she/it/usted with 'quiere' and demonstrates question formation through intonation. Additionally, students learn the motion verb 'venir' (requiring 'a' before an infinitive) and the verb 'debo' to convey obligation ('must').

ord.en: he wants / she wants / it wants / you (formal) want

fraser.en: I want to see it / I want to see her.
Do you want to visit me?
You don't want to visit me.
Don't you want to visit me?
Why don't you want to visit me?
Do you want to come to the house?
Do you want to come to visit me?
Don't you want to come to visit me?

fraser.es: ¿Por qué no quiere venir a visitarme?
fraser.en: Why don't you want to come to visit me?

koncept: Feminine direct object pronoun 'la' and plural object pronouns 'los'/'las'
Third-person and formal second-person shared verb forms ('quiere')
Question formation via intonation rather than auxiliary verbs
Using the preposition 'a' with motion verbs ('venir a')
Expressing obligation/necessity using 'debo' + infinitive

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the verb 'saber' (to know) and the conjunction 'si' (if), combining them into compound sentence structures with previously learned vocabulary. It reinforces breaking long, complex sentences into manageable thought blocks and maintaining verb-preposition links across clause boundaries. It also covers vocabulary expansion via cognates with spelling adjustments ('explicación' / 'explicar') and attaching pronouns to infinitives.

fraser.en: Why doesn't he/she/you want to know?

fraser.es: Quiero saber por qué no quiere saber.
fraser.en: I want to know why he doesn't want to know.
I want to know if you/he/she want(s) to know.
I want to know if he/she wants to invite me.
I don't want to imagine it.

fraser.es: Quiero saber si quiere venir a la casa a visitarme.
fraser.en: I want to know if she wants to come to the house to visit me.

fraser.es: Quiero saber por qué no quiere venir a la casa a visitarme.
fraser.en: I want to know why she doesn't want to come to the house to visit me.

fraser.es: Voy a invitarlo, pero no voy a invitarlo ahora.
fraser.en: I am going to invite him/you, but I'm not going to invite him/you now.
I want to start it now.
Why doesn't he/she want to inform me / let me know?

fraser.es: No intento justificarme, pero quiero explicarte algo.
fraser.en: I am not trying to justify myself, but I want to explain something to you.

koncept: The verb saber (to know) and cognate connection to British slang 'savvy' / Latin root
Using 'si' for 'if' (homophone with 'sí' for 'yes')
Connecting motion verbs like 'venir' with preposition 'a' before an infinitive ('venir a la casa a visitarme')
Reflexive/object pronouns attached to infinitives ('justificarme', 'explicarte')
Cognate conversion patterns: -tion to -ción exceptions ('explanation' -> 'explicación', 'explain' -> 'explicar')

lektioner.om: The lesson covers verb classification (-ar, -er, -ir) and explains how regular 'yo' forms are created by swapping the ending for '-o' with stress shifting to the penultimate syllable. It introduces key vocabulary like comer, tener, and time words (tarde, más tarde, mañana), showing how present tense can imply the future when context is given. Finally, it explores verbs related to tener (-tain cognates) and shows the irregular 'yo' pattern shared by tener (tengo) and venir (vengo).

fraser.en: I'm eating tomorrow / I eat tomorrow.

fraser.es: Voy a comer con Pablo mañana.
fraser.en: I'm going to eat with Pablo tomorrow.
I am going to have it late.
I am going to have it later.

koncept: Infinitive verb endings in Spanish (-ar, -er, -ir)
Forming the regular present 'I' (yo) form by dropping the infinitive ending and adding -o
Stress shift to the penultimate syllable in present tense forms
Using present tense with future time markers (e.g., mañana) to express future actions
Irregular 'yo' forms with 'g' insertion (tener -> tengo, venir -> vengo)
Cognate prefixes attached to -tener (contener, obtener, sostener, mantener, entretener)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces present tense conjugations for -ar verbs, showing how the characteristic vowel 'a' is modified for different subject pronouns (-o for yo, -a for él/ella/usted, -an for ellos/ustedes, and -as for tú). It also explains the placement of direct object pronouns, which must precede a conjugated verb alone, but can either precede the conjugated verb or attach to the end of an infinitive in verb pairs.

fraser.en: It lasts a long time / it lasts much.
It doesn't last a long time.
He/she is not exaggerating / you (formal) are not exaggerating.
They don't speak with Pablo / They're not speaking with Pablo.
I want to see it / I want to see him.
It's important to speak about it.

koncept: -ar verb conjugation in present tense (-o, -a, -an, -as)
Object pronoun placement (before conjugated verb or attached to infinitive)
Silent 'h' in Spanish (hablar)
Word conversion via Latin roots (duration -> durar, mastication -> masticar)

lektioner.om: The lesson contrasts -ar verbs with -er/-ir verbs, establishing 'e' as the characteristic vowel for the latter group. It introduces patterns for feminine noun endings (-ión, -idad) and shows how to derive adjectives from nouns by stripping endings. Finally, it teaches how to place double object pronouns before conjugated verbs, putting the personal pronoun first (e.g., 'me lo venden', 'nos lo venden').

fraser.en: I sell it. / I am selling it.
I sell them. / I am selling them (masculine/mixed).
I sell them. / I am selling them (feminine).
He/she sells it. / You (formal) sell it.
They sell it to me. / They are selling it to me.
They don't sell it to me.
Why don't they sell it to me?
They are not selling it to us.
Why don't they sell it to us?

koncept: Present tense conjugation of -er/-ir verbs using the key vowel 'e' (vende, venden)
Gender of nouns: words ending in -a, -ión, and -idad are feminine (taking 'la')
Converting English '-ity' words to Spanish '-idad' and stripping suffixes to form adjectives
Object pronoun combining and ordering: personal pronoun before object pronoun (me lo, nos lo)

lektioner.om: Introduces the verbs 'hacer', 'poder', and 'esperar', reinforcing how to conjugate for informal 'you' (-s) and 'they' (-n). Explains the importance of checking the infinitive ending (-ar vs -er/-ir) to avoid vowel confusion. Introduces the vocabulary conversion rule for English words ending in '-ary' turning into '-ario'.

fraser.en: They / you guys are doing it.
What are you doing? / What are you up to?

fraser.es: Quiero saber por qué no puedes venir.
fraser.en: I want to know why you can't come.
They are not waiting for me.

fraser.es: Quiero saber por qué no me esperan.
fraser.en: I want to know why they are not waiting for me.

koncept: Informal 'you' (tú) ending with -s (haces, puedes)
They/plural 'you' ending with -n (hacen, esperan)
Modal verb 'poder' followed by infinitive without preposition
Irregular first-person '-go' verbs (salgo, vengo, tengo)
Avoiding false vowel harmony by referencing the infinitive (-ar vs -er/-ir)
Transitive use of 'esperar' (waiting for someone = esperar a alguien / me esperan)
English to Spanish suffix conversion: -ary to -ario

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the irregular 'yo' form 'sé' (saber) and the irregular '-go' first-person present verbs like 'salgo', 'pongo', and related compound verbs (suponer -> supongo, oponer -> opongo). It explains how explicit subject pronouns (él, ella, yo) are used selectively for emphasis or contrast. Additionally, it teaches 'tener que + infinitive' for expressing everyday obligation alongside 'deber', and reviews helper verbs followed by infinitives.

ord.en: I can / I am able to

fraser.en: I don't know what he wants.
I don't know what he wants (emphatic).

fraser.es: No quiero invitarlo, pero ella sí.
fraser.en: I don't want to invite him, but she does.

fraser.es: Yo no quiero invitarlo, pero ella sí.
fraser.en: I don't want to invite him, but she does (emphatic).
When are you coming to eat?
I want to know what you/he/she have/has.

fraser.es: Voy a intentar comer más tarde.
fraser.en: I'm going to try to eat later.

koncept: Irregular first-person singular '-go' verbs (salgo, tengo, vengo, pongo, supongo, opongo, obtengo)
Explicit subject pronouns (él, ella, yo) used for contrast and emphasis
Obligation structures: 'tener que + infinitive' (everyday have to) vs. 'deber + infinitive' (moral/serious must)
Verbs of motion taking 'a' before an infinitive (voy a comer, salgo a comer, vienes a comer)
English verb root cognates (-pose -> -poner, -tain -> -tener)
Modal/helper verbs followed directly by an infinitive (quiero, puedo, debo, voy a, tengo que)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains the systematic stem change where stressed 'e' in a verb root splits into 'ie' across present tense conjugations (e.g., pensar -> pienso, entender -> entiendo, perder -> pierdo). It also introduces 'pensar + infinitive' for expressing intentions ('I plan to...'), using cognates like tempo/tiempo and concert/concierto to illustrate the vowel shift.

ord.en: to pass, to happen, to occur

fraser.en: What is happening? / What's going on?
I want to know what's happening.
I plan on eating. / I think to eat.

koncept: Stem-changing / vowel splitting (e -> ie) under stress in the present tense
Using 'pensar + infinitive' to express planning or intending to do something
Distinction between base infinitive endings (-ar, -er, -ir) when conjugating stem-changing verbs

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces boot verbs / stem-changing verbs where root vowels split when stressed in the present tense: E splits to IE (empezar -> empieza) and O splits to UE (dormir -> duerme, encontrar -> encuentra, mostrar -> muestra). The instructor connects the O -> UE sound shift to English cognates (port/puerto, force/fuerza, corp/cuerpo, novel/nuevo). The lesson also highlights how verb forms can double as nouns (un encuentro, una muestra, el poder) and introduces the reflexive meaning of dormirse ('to fall asleep').

ord.en: to find, to encounter, to meet

fraser.en: I fall asleep. / I'm falling asleep.

koncept: Stem-changing verbs: E -> IE (empezar -> empiezo)
Stem-changing verbs: O -> UE (dormir -> duermo, encontrar -> encuentro, mostrar -> muestro)
Reflexive verbs for state changes (dormir vs. dormirse)
Nouns derived from verb forms (el poder, un encuentro, una muestra)

lektioner.om: This lesson explores stem-vowel splitting (e -> ie and o -> ue) as a direct result of word stress, demonstrating how verbs like perder, colgar, encontrar, mostrar, pensar, and cerrar split in stressed forms. It introduces the 'we' (-amos) ending for -ar verbs, showing that the vowel does not split because the stress shifts to the ending. Additionally, the lesson discusses the Arabic linguistic influence on Spanish vocabulary (e.g., words beginning with 'al-' and assimilating consonants like arroz and azúcar).

fraser.en: What do you plan on doing?

koncept: Stem-vowel splitting (e -> ie, o -> ue) driven by stress
Arabic origin of words starting with al- / assimilated consonants
First person plural (we / nosotros) verb conjugation ending in -amos for -ar verbs
Lack of stem splitting in the 'we' form due to stress falling on the ending syllable

lektioner.om: Introduces the only grammatical distinction between -er and -ir verbs in the entire language: the 'nosotros' present tense endings (-emos vs. -imos). Highlights the Spanish pronunciation of 'v' and 'b' and introduces new verbs such as 'vivir', 'preferir', and 'entender'.

fraser.es: no vivo aquí, pero él vive aquí
fraser.en: I don't live here, but he lives here
I want to know where they live

fraser.es: quiero saber por qué no entiende
fraser.en: I want to know why he doesn't understand

koncept: Distinction between -er (-emos) and -ir (-imos) verbs in the 'nosotros' present tense
Pronunciation of 'b' and 'v' in Spanish (soft bilabial fricative)
Stem-changing verbs (preferir -> prefiero, entender -> entiendo) not splitting in the nosotros form
Using 'aquí' vs 'acá'
Question words 'dónde' and 'por qué' in embedded clauses

lektioner.om: This lesson teaches how to reverse-engineer verb conjugations from known forms like 'vamos' to discover 'va', 'vas', and 'van', and introduces the infinitive 'ir'. It covers 'tener que + infinitive' for expressing obligation, as well as context clues for determining the gender of nouns ending in '-e' such as 'noche' and 'carne'.

fraser.es: No como carne y no tomo alcohol.
fraser.en: I don't eat meat and I don't drink alcohol.
I eat meat and I drink alcohol.

koncept: Vowel splitting comparison across Romance languages (e -> ie in siempre, bien, etc.)
Working backwards from conjugated forms (vamos -> va, vas, van)
The infinitive of 'to go' (ir) and its historical etymology
Obligation structure: tener que + infinitive
Gender of nouns ending in -e (determined by surrounding context like articles/demonstratives)
Silent 'h' in Spanish pronunciation (alcohol)

lektioner.om: The teacher reviews how the present tense expresses future actions when paired with time markers like 'pronto' (soon) or 'la semana que viene' (next week). The lesson introduces the verb 'ver' (with irregular 'veo') and practices object pronoun placement ('nos', 'la', 'las', 'lo') both in the present tense and with 'ir a + infinitive'. Finally, the teacher highlights reciprocal 'nos' in expressions like 'nos vemos' and emphasizes building sentences thought-by-thought rather than memorizing entire phrases.

fraser.en: Why aren't you seeing them (female) soon?
We are going to see her.
Are you going to see him soon?

fraser.es: ¿Vas a vernos pronto? / ¿Nos vas a ver pronto?
fraser.en: Are you going to see us soon?

fraser.es: ¿Por qué no vas a vernos pronto?
fraser.en: Why aren't you going to see us soon?
See you / We see each other (goodbye).

fraser.es: Nos vemos la semana que viene.
fraser.en: We will see each other next week / See you next week.

koncept: Using present tense with future context (pronto, más tarde, la semana que viene)
Conjugating 'ver' in the present tense (veo, ve, ven, ves, vemos)
Using 'ir a + infinitive' to talk about the future
Object pronoun placement with compound verb structures (before conjugated verb or attached to infinitive)
Using 'nos' for reciprocal actions ('each other') and reflexive meaning ('ourselves')
Constructing 'next week' as 'la semana que viene' (the week that comes)

lektioner.om: Introduces the present perfect tense in Spanish using the auxiliary verb haber and -ado past participles for -ar verbs. The instructor explains the irregular forms of haber using the vowels 'e' and 'a' found in the infinitive stem. Students practice combining haber with past participles and properly placing object pronouns before the auxiliary verb.

fraser.es: Lo hemos anticipado por mucho tiempo.
fraser.en: We have anticipated it for a long time.
Have you celebrated? / Did you celebrate?

koncept: present perfect tense (pretérito perfecto compuesto)
conjugation of auxiliary verb haber (he, has, ha, hemos, han)
forming past participles of -ar verbs with -ado
object pronoun placement before auxiliary haber (e.g., lo hemos anticipado)

lektioner.om: The lesson builds on the present perfect tense using haber with past participles ending in -ado and -ido. It establishes the rule for object pronoun placement with compound tenses (before the conjugated auxiliary verb 'haber') and clearly differentiates subject pronouns from object pronouns across all grammatical persons.

fraser.en: I see it / I see him.
I see her / I see it (feminine).

koncept: Present perfect formation with haber + past participle (-ado for -ar verbs, -ido for -er/-ir verbs)
Object pronoun placement before the conjugated auxiliary verb 'haber'
Distinction between subject pronouns (yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros/as, ellos/ellas) and object pronouns (me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las)
Subject pronoun flexibility in word order (e.g. usted lo ve vs. lo ve usted)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains why Greek-origin nouns ending in -ma are masculine (el problema, el sistema) rather than feminine. It also teaches how to express 'getting lost' using the reflexive form of perder (perderse) conjugated in the present perfect tense with haber.

ord.en: to feel / to perceive / to smell

fraser.en: I have got lost / I have lost myself.
You have got lost / You have lost yourself. (informal)
We have got lost / We have lost ourselves.

koncept: Masculine nouns ending in -ma derived from Greek (el problema, el sistema, el programa, el aroma, el clima)
Reflexive verbs with the perfect tense to express 'getting' (perderse = to get lost / to lose oneself -> me he perdido, te has perdido, nos hemos perdido)
Subject pronoun emphasis with compound reflexive past tenses (yo me he perdido, tú te has perdido, nosotros nos hemos perdido)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the verb 'dar' (to give) and its present tense forms, highlighting the irregular first-person 'doy'. The teacher explains double object pronoun placement, showing that personal pronouns precede object pronouns (e.g., 'me lo', 'te lo'). It also covers expressing future intentions using the present tense with time markers like 'mañana', the plural pronoun 'ustedes', and word order flexibility for subject emphasis.

fraser.en: He gives me something / He is giving me something.
They give it to me (emphasizing they).
I will give it to you tomorrow / I give it to you tomorrow.
Are you giving it to me tomorrow? (formal)
Are you giving it to me tomorrow? (formal, emphatic)
They / you guys give it to us tomorrow.
Are you guys giving it to us tomorrow?
I want to give it to you.

koncept: Conjugation of the irregular verb 'dar' (doy, das, da, dan)
Double object pronoun order (indirect/person before direct/thing: me lo, te lo, nos lo)
Using the present tense with future context (mañana) to express future actions
Pluralizing nouns/pronouns ending in consonants with '-es' (usted -> ustedes)
Pronoun placement with compound verb structures (te lo quiero dar)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how indirect object pronouns in Spanish absorb English prepositions like 'to', 'for', and 'from'. It introduces cooking vocabulary (la cocina, cocinar), numbers 8–10 (ocho, nueve, diez), and time expressions using 'a las'. Finally, it presents the reflexive verb quedarse ('to stay/remain oneself') and illustrates how subject pronouns can be added for extra emphasis alongside mandatory reflexive pronouns.

fraser.en: He speaks to me. / He is speaking to me.
They speak to me about it.
Shall I buy it for you? / Shall I buy it from you?
Do you want to do it?
Do you want to do it for me?
Can you cook something for me?
I have cooked at six o'clock. / I cooked at six o'clock.
We have cooked at eight o'clock.

fraser.es: Me quedo aquí hasta las diez.

koncept: Object pronouns (me, te, nos) encompassing 'to me', 'for me', and 'from me' without extra prepositions
Expressing 'shall I...' using present tense question intonation
Telling time with 'a las [hora]'
Reflexive meaning with quedar (quedarse = to stay / remain oneself)
Combining reflexive pronouns with subject pronouns for emphasis (yo me quedo, tú te quedas, nosotros nos quedamos)
Spelling rule for 'qu' producing a hard 'k' sound in Spanish

lektioner.om: This lesson consolidates reflexive pronoun placement with compound verb structures, modal auxiliaries, and the present perfect. It introduces 'tener que' for expressing obligation and 'pensar' for plans/intentions. Finally, it demystifies common introduction phrases by analyzing 'llamarse' reflexively.

fraser.es: Voy a quedarme hasta las siete.
Quiero saber por qué tienes que quedarte aquí.
fraser.en: I want to know why you have to stay here.
Do you plan on staying here tonight?
What is your name? (How do you call yourself?)

koncept: Reflexive pronoun placement (attached to infinitive or before changed verb/auxiliary)
Expressing obligation with 'tener que + infinitive' vs 'deber'
Using 'pensar + infinitive' to express planning or intending to do something
Reflexive usage of 'llamar' for introducing oneself ('llamarse')

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces descriptive adjective placement following the noun and reinforces adjective agreement in number (plural -s/es). It explains regional synonyms for 'car' (coche, carro, auto, máquina) to illustrate that gender belongs to the specific noun rather than the physical object. The teacher also highlights communicative 'thought shortcuts' using modal constructions like 'puedo' + infinitive before practicing reflexive actions in present and perfect tenses.

fraser.en: I want to buy a digital camera.
I want to buy the digital camera.
the big car / the big machine
Do you see the big car?
Can you see the big car?
I don't find it / I can't find it.

fraser.es: Me quedo en el auto rojo.
fraser.en: I am staying in the red car.

fraser.es: Me he quedado en el auto rojo.
fraser.en: I have stayed in the red car.
I have bought a red car.

fraser.es: Me he comprado un auto rojo.
fraser.en: I have bought myself a red car.

koncept: Adjective placement after nouns (la situación global, el auto rojo)
Plural agreement for nouns, articles, and adjectives (las casas grandes, los autos grandes)
Gender agreement for articles with masculine/feminine nouns (el/la, un/una, los/las)
Alternative vocabulary across Spanish dialects (coche, carro, auto, máquina)
Mental shortcuts using modal/semi-auxiliary verbs (puedo encontrarlo vs no lo encuentro, puedes ver vs ves)
Reflexive pronoun placement with conjugated verbs and past perfect (me quedo, me he quedado, me he comprado)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the plural form 'son' and explores the conversion rule from English words ending in '-ive' to Spanish '-ivo'/'-iva'. It also covers how nouns ending in consonants form feminine counterparts (by adding '-a') and plural forms (by adding '-es'), while highlighting the difference between nouns and adjectives regarding gender inflection.

fraser.en: It is expensive (referring to a feminine noun).

koncept: Difference between single 'r' (caro) and rolled 'rr' (carro)
Plural article 'los' (from 'el') and plural endings with -es for words ending in consonants (profesores, doctores)
Gender modification for nouns (profesor/profesora, doctor/doctora) vs. adjectives
Third person plural 'son' (they are / you all are)
English -ive conversion to Spanish -ivo/-iva
Spelling rule: English double consonants (except rr, nn, cc, ll) simplify to single consonants in Spanish

lektioner.om: Introduces the verb 'estar' and explains the fundamental distinction between 'ser' (characteristics/identity) and 'estar' (states/conditions). Emphasizes avoiding the misleading 'permanent vs. temporary' rule, illustrating with examples like professions (ser) and death (estar). Presents the present tense conjugation of 'estar' and practices adjectives like 'cansado' and 'muerto'.
koncept: Distinction between ser (characteristic/essence) and estar (state/condition)
Why 'permanent vs temporary' is an inaccurate simplification for ser vs estar
Conjugation of estar in the present tense (estoy, estás, está, estamos, están)
Stress/accentuation pattern of estar (accent on the last syllable in present tense)

lektioner.om: This lesson covers the question words 'cómo' and 'dónde' paired with conjugations of 'estar' for locations and states. It also reviews modal expressions of obligation and probability using 'tener que' and 'deber', alongside adjective agreement. Finally, it introduces the reflexive concept for 'staying' with 'quedarse' and demonstrates pronoun placement with auxiliary verb structures.

fraser.en: I don't know where we are.

fraser.es: Voy a estar aquí más tarde.
fraser.en: I am going to be here later.
Where are you going to be? (informal)
Where do you have to be later? (plural)

fraser.es: No vamos a quedarnos porque estamos muy cansados.
fraser.en: We are not going to stay because we are very tired.

koncept: Interrogative adverbs (cómo, dónde)
Conjugations of estar with subject pronouns for emphasis
Expressing probability or duty with deber + infinitive
Obligation with tener que + infinitive
Reflexive verb usage with quedar/quedarse and pronoun placement options

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the second Spanish verb for 'to be', 'ser', contrasting its use for characteristics with 'estar' for states. The teacher explains Spanish phonotactics adding an initial 'e-' before 's+consonant' clusters and conjugates 'ser' across all subject pronouns. Finally, the practical distinction is demonstrated by comparing '¿Cómo está?' (how is he doing) with '¿Cómo es?' (what is he like).

fraser.en: How is he? / How is he doing?

koncept: Initial e- before s+consonant clusters in Spanish (español, escuela, estricto)
The verb 'ser' for characteristics vs. 'estar' for states
Full conjugation of 'ser' in present tense (soy, eres, es, somos, son)
Four Spanish verbs ending in -oy for 'yo' (voy, doy, estoy, soy)
Contrast between '¿Cómo está?' (state/well-being) and '¿Cómo es?' (characteristic/personality)

lektioner.om: This lesson explores how the meaning of adjectives changes when paired with 'ser' (characteristic) versus 'estar' (state), using examples like 'aburrido' (boring vs. bored). It introduces the preposition 'de' for origin questions ('¿De dónde eres?') and demonstrates how to use 'persona' as a grammatical safety net with 'ser' to describe inherent personality traits.

fraser.en: Where is he from? / Where are you (formal) from?

koncept: Ser vs. estar with adjectives (state vs. characteristic changes meaning: aburrido, libre)
Origin questions using 'de dónde' + ser
Using 'persona' + adjective as a safe construction with 'ser' for characteristics
Adjective agreement with grammatically feminine nouns like 'persona'

lektioner.om: This lesson explores adjectives that shift meaning depending on whether they pair with ser (characteristic) or estar (state), such as listo (smart vs. ready), aburrido (boring vs. bored), and bueno (good-natured/skilled vs. attractive). It introduces the adverb 'tan' (so) and discusses how to express happiness using 'feliz' with both verbs or via 'soy una persona feliz'.

ord.en: good; good person / skilled (with ser); attractive / hot / in good shape (with estar for people)

fraser.en: you are very smart (to a female)

fraser.es: estoy tan cansado / estoy tan cansada
estoy tan aburrido / estoy tan aburrida

fraser.en: he is good (a good person / good at something)
he is attractive / in good shape
I want to know how he is doing
I want to know what he is like

koncept: Adjectives whose meanings change with ser vs. estar (e.g., listo, aburrido, bueno, feliz)
Ser vs. estar with people (character vs. state/attractiveness)
Intensifier 'tan' (so)
Expressing personality traits vs. temporary emotional states

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the Spanish gerund and the present continuous tense constructed with estar (e.g., estoy hablando, están comiendo). The teacher clarifies the crucial difference in usage between English and Spanish: Spanish only uses the continuous form for actions taking place right at that exact moment, relying on the simple present for future plans. Students also practice placing direct object pronouns either preceding estar or suffixed directly to the gerund.

fraser.en: I am preparing it tomorrow / I'll prepare it tomorrow.
I am preparing it later / I will prepare it later.

koncept: Gerund formation (-ando for -ar verbs, -iendo for -er/-ir verbs)
Present continuous tense with estar + gerund (used strictly for actions happening right now)
Contrast between simple present for planned future actions vs present continuous for ongoing actions
Object pronoun placement with gerunds (before estar or attached to the end of the gerund)

lektioner.om: The lesson explores combining estar with the gerund 'siendo' to express temporary behavior of inherent characteristics (such as being honest or sincere right now). It also warns against negative language transfer from English, showing that simple present is used in Spanish for planned near-future events, reserving the -ando/-iendo continuous form strictly for actions happening in the immediate moment.

ord.en: next week (literally: the week that comes)

fraser.es: Los compro la semana que viene.

koncept: Difference between ser (characteristics) and estar (states)
Using 'estar + siendo' for temporary behavior (being sincere/honest)
Avoiding English -ing interference: simple present tense for near future actions versus continuous present for actions occurring right now
Clitic pronoun placement with gerunds (los estoy comprando / estoy comprándolos)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the synthetic future tense in Spanish. The teacher explains that the endings for all verbs (-ar, -er, -ir) are identical to the present tense forms of haber (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án) attached directly to the full infinitive. Students practice converting infinitives like comer, ir, encontrar, and preparar into their future forms.

ord.en: I will wait / I will hope
he/she/it will organize / you (formal) will organize

fraser.en: I'm having breakfast with them tomorrow.
I am going to have breakfast with them.

koncept: Future tense formation by attaching haber endings (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án) to the infinitive
Stress pattern in the future tense (accent pushed to the final syllable/ending)
Comparison between present tense with future context, 'ir a + infinitive', and the synthetic future tense
Regularity of 'ir' in the future tense (iré, irás, irá, iremos, irán)
Reflexive verbs in the future tense (e.g., 'me quedaré')

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the contrast between direct object pronouns (lo, la, los, las) and indirect object pronouns (le, les), emphasizing the underlying grammatical feeling of 'to' or 'for' someone rather than relying on English translations. It covers pronoun ordering when combining direct and indirect pronouns (the personal pronoun always comes first) and explains how 'me', 'te', and 'nos' remain unchanged in both roles. Additionally, the idiom 'darse cuenta' is introduced and contrasted with 'realizar'.

ord.en: to carry out / to fulfill / to bring into fruition

fraser.en: Will you guys give it to me?
They will give it to you.
They will give it to us.
They will not give it to us.
Do you realize? / Do you know what I mean?
I have spoken to him / her.
We have spoken to him / her.
He is cooking him / her something.
He is cooking them for us.

koncept: Future tense of 'dar' (daré, daremos, dará, darán, darás)
Direct vs. Indirect object pronouns (lo/la/los/las vs. le/les)
Pronoun order: personal pronoun comes before the object pronoun (me lo, te lo, nos las)
Reflexive and idiomatic expression 'darse cuenta' (to realize)
Dative of benefit / indirect object usage with verbs like 'cocinar' and 'hablar'
Present perfect tense with 'haber' + past participle (he hablado, le han hablado)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the reflexive pronoun 'se' representing himself, herself, itself, themselves, and oneself, contrasting it with 'me', 'te', and 'nos'. The teacher explains how dictionary entries list reflexive verbs with '-se' when doing an action to oneself changes the verb's core meaning, using 'quedarse' (to stay) and 'darse cuenta' (to realize) as primary examples.

fraser.en: We speak to ourselves / We speak to each other.
He speaks to himself / She speaks to herself.
He stays / She stays / You (formal) stay.
He wants to stay / She wants to stay.
They want to stay / You guys want to stay.
He realizes / She realizes / You (formal) realize.
They don't realize / You guys don't realize.

koncept: Reflexive pronoun 'se' for third-person (himself, herself, themselves, oneself)
Comparison between indirect pronoun 'les' and reflexive pronoun 'se'
Reflexive verbs with shifting meaning ('quedarse', 'darse cuenta')
Attaching reflexive pronouns to infinitives ('quedarme', 'quedarse')
Dictionary format of reflexive verbs (-se ending)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces prepositional pronoun usage in Spanish, explaining that subject pronouns are generally kept after prepositions (with the notable exceptions of 'mí' and 'ti'). It also illustrates the difference between 'es' and 'está' when expressing origin/purpose versus location with prepositions. Finally, it demonstrates how indirect object pronouns naturally absorb English prepositions like 'for' and 'from'.

fraser.en: He is doing me a favor.
He is doing her a favor.
I buy for them / I buy them (indirect object).
He buys it for me / He buys it from me.

koncept: Pronouns after prepositions (él, ella, ellos, nosotros, usted, ustedes vs. special forms mí and ti)
Ser vs. Estar with prepositions (characteristics with 'de'/'para' vs. location/state with 'con')
Indirect object pronouns (le, les, me, te, nos) absorbing prepositions like 'to', 'for', and 'from'
Double object pronoun placement (me lo compra, me los compran)

lektioner.om: This lesson focuses on how verbs pair with different prepositions in Spanish compared to English, such as 'enamorarse de' (fall in love with), 'pensar en' (think about), 'soñar con' (dream about), and 'depender de' (depend on). It introduces the irregular stem change in 'soñar' (sueño) and the Spanish letter 'ñ'. It also covers the combined forms 'conmigo' and 'contigo', and using 'si' to mean 'if'.

fraser.en: I fall in love with you.
I fall in love with him.
Do you want to come with me?
Why don't you want to come with me?
You have to come with me.
It depends on if she wants to go.

koncept: Differences in verb-preposition pairings between English and Spanish (enamorarse de, pensar en, soñar con, depender de)
Stem-changing verbs (o -> ue in soñar: sueño, sueñas, sueña, sueñan vs soñamos)
Special prepositional pronoun forms with con (conmigo, contigo)
Using 'si' for 'if' (identical pronunciation to 'sí' for 'yes')

lektioner.om: This lesson reviews the future tense formed by attaching the endings of haber to the infinitive and introduces the conditional ('would') tense formed by attaching -ía endings to the infinitive across all verb groups. It also explains how the reflexive pronoun 'se' serves to express the English concept of 'getting [done/transformed]' where Spanish lacks a direct verb for 'to get'.

fraser.en: We dance later / We will dance later.
We are going to dance later.
I would eat, but I don't have time.

fraser.es: Me imaginaría que no quiere ir.
fraser.en: I would imagine that he doesn't want to go.

koncept: Future tense endings (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án) derived from the present tense of haber added to the infinitive
Conditional tense endings (-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -ían) added to the infinitive for all verb classes (-ar, -er, -ir)
Use of reflexive pronoun 'se' to express passive/inchoative 'get + adjective/participle' (e.g., se contamina, se transformaría)
Reflexive verbs used idiomatically without altering fundamental meaning (e.g., me imagino)

lektioner.om: This lesson explores the conditional tense ('would') with verbs like 'hablar', then introduces the verb 'gustar' by reframing it literally as 'to be pleasing' to avoid common learner mistakes like saying 'me gusto'. It also introduces the irregular contracted conditional stem 'podr-' for 'poder' ('podría' = 'could' / 'would be able to') and practices forming polite requests.

ord.en: to be pleasing / to please (to like)

fraser.en: I would like. (It would please me.)
I would like to eat now.
We would like to eat now.
I would like to see you.
Could you come to my house?
Could you tell me if you want to come?

koncept: Conditional tense endings (-ía, -ías, -íamos, -ían)
The structure and mechanics of 'gustar' (literally 'to be pleasing to')
Irregular conditional/future stem contraction of 'poder' -> 'podr-'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the conditional perfect construction using 'habría' (from the contracted conditional form of haber) combined with past participles to express 'would have'. It explores expressions with gustar in the conditional perfect ('me habría gustado') and explains how 'debería' functions as 'should'. The lesson finishes with practicing the conditional of 'dar' with object pronouns.

fraser.en: We would have been able to go.
They would have been able to eat.
They would have come to eat.
I would have liked it (It would have pleased me).
We would have liked it (It would have pleased us).
We would have liked them (They would have pleased us).
You should come to my house.

fraser.es: Deberías venir a mi casa a comer.
fraser.en: You should come to my house to eat.
We should speak to him / her / you (formal).
We should speak to them / you all.
They would give it to me.

koncept: Conditional perfect tense with contracted auxiliary verb haber (habría, habríamos, habrían + participle)
Conditional modal with deber (debería = should)
Using the infinitive following modal verbs rather than participle
Conditional tense of dar (daría, darían) with object pronouns

lektioner.om: This lesson explores gender exceptions in Spanish nouns, focusing on masculine Greek loanwords ending in '-ma' or '-ta' (el sistema, el planeta) and feminine nouns ending in '-o' (la mano, shortened forms like la foto). It introduces demonstratives ('este/esta' vs 'ese/esa') and practices building sentences with modal verbs, idioms ('dar una mano'), and the present continuous.

ord.en: to manage / to handle / to drive

fraser.es: No quiero ese auto porque es muy grande.
fraser.en: I don't want that car because it's very big.
Can you give me a hand?
Could you give me a hand?
You should give me a hand.
You (plural) should give me a hand.
You (plural) should give us a hand.

fraser.es: Me gustaría tomar una foto, pero no tengo mi cámara.
fraser.en: I would like to take a photo, but I don't have my camera.

koncept: Gender exceptions in nouns (Greek-origin masculine nouns ending in -ma/-ta like el problema, el sistema, el planeta; feminine nouns ending in -o like la mano, la foto)
Demonstrative adjectives (este/esta/estos/estas for 'this/these', ese/esa/esos/esas for 'that/those')
Idiomatic expression 'dar una mano' (to give a hand)
Gerund / continuous present construction (estar + -ando / -iendo)
Conditional tense with modal verbs (podrías, deberías, me gustaría)

lektioner.om: This lesson extends the structure of 'gustar' to other verbs like 'interesar' and 'parecer', emphasizing that indirect object pronouns ('le', 'les') are used because the actions mean 'to be pleasing/interesting/seeming to someone'. It also explores using 'le'/'les' with 'poner' to mean putting something 'on it' or 'on them', and covers the connection between English verbs ending in -pose and Spanish verbs ending in -poner.

ord.en: to interest / to be interesting to

fraser.en: She likes it / He likes it.
He likes them / She likes them.

fraser.es: ¿Le interesa salir a bailar esta noche?
fraser.en: Does it interest her to go out to dance tonight?
It seems good to me / It seems fine to me.

fraser.es: Me parece que no quiere salir esta noche.
fraser.en: It seems to me that he doesn't want to go out tonight.
It would interest me to see it.
I want to put salt on it.

fraser.es: Me gustaría ponerle un poco más sal.
fraser.en: I would like to put a little more salt on it.

fraser.es: Me gustaría ponerles un poco más sal.
fraser.en: I would like to put a little more salt on them.

koncept: Verbs functioning like gustar (interesar, parecer) taking indirect object pronouns (me, te, le, nos, les)
Using 'le' and 'les' to represent 'on it' / 'on them' or 'to it' / 'to them' with verbs like poner
Connecting clauses using obligatory 'que' (that)
English verbs ending in -pose translating to -poner (componer, suponer, oponer, imponer)

lektioner.om: This lesson outlines the three past frameworks in Spanish, comparing the perfect past (haber + participle), the imperfect 'line in the past' (ongoing/habitual), and the preterite 'dot in the past'. The teacher reviews the compound perfect and conditional perfect with haber (habría), then introduces the imperfect tense for -ar verbs using the -aba endings across all subject persons.

fraser.en: I have been able to eat.
I haven't been able to eat.
I would have been able to go out.
I wouldn't have been able to go out.
I / he / she was speaking / used to speak.
You were speaking / used to speak (informal).
They / you guys were speaking / used to speak.
We were speaking / used to speak.
I was waiting for you (formal m/f).
We were waiting for you guys / for them.
They were trying to find it.
They were trying to find it for me (natural).
They were trying to find it for me (emphatic).

koncept: three past frameworks in Spanish: perfect (he comido), imperfect line (comía/hablaba), and preterite dot (comí/hablé)
conditional perfect: habría + participle (habría salido, habría podido salir)
imperfect tense for -ar verbs: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -aban
pronoun placement on infinitives with double pronouns (encontrármelo) vs. prepositional phrases (para mí)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how Spanish uses reflexive pronouns (me, se) with verbs like quemar and romper to express intransitive states or 'getting' done (e.g., getting burned, getting broken). It also contrasts these structures with transitive usages where a direct object is present. Finally, it introduces masculine demonstratives (este/estos, ese/esos) and their logical connection to definite articles (el/los).

fraser.en: The dinner was burning / getting burned.
I get burnt in the sun.

fraser.es: Esos se rompen todo el tiempo.
fraser.en: Those ones break all the time.

koncept: imperfect tense with -aba for -ar verbs
reflexive pronoun 'se' / 'me' used for inchoative/intransitive actions ('getting burned', 'breaking')
flexible word order in Spanish compared to English
masculine demonstrative adjectives and pronouns: este/estos (this/these) and ese/esos (that/those)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the imperfect tense for -er/-ir verbs using the ending -ía, highlighting how it differs from the conditional (which attaches to the infinitive). It also explores the diverse uses of the pronoun 'se'—including passive/impersonal expressions like 'se vende' and '¿cómo se dice?'. Finally, the teacher contrasts 'quedar' (to remain / to have left over) with reflexive 'quedarse' (to stay) across both present and imperfect tenses.

fraser.en: It is for sale. / It sells itself.
How do you say? / How is it said?

koncept: Imperfect tense (-ía) for -er and -ir verbs contrasted with the conditional tense (-ería)
Imperfect tense (-aba) for -ar verbs
Passive and impersonal use of 'se' (e.g., 'se vende', '¿cómo se dice?')
Reflexive verb 'quedarse' (to stay) vs intransitive 'quedar' with indirect object pronouns to express remaining / having left (e.g., 'me queda uno')

lektioner.om: This lesson reviews the imperfect tense for habitual or continuous past actions with verbs like llamar and tener. It introduces the only three irregular verbs in the Spanish imperfect: ver (veía), ser (era), and ir (iba). Finally, it demonstrates how to use iba a + infinitive to express what someone 'was going to do'.

fraser.en: What is your name? / How do you call yourself?
I used to have a big house.
We used to have a big house.

fraser.es: Tenía cuatro, pero ahora no me queda.
fraser.en: I used to have four, but now I don't have any left.
I had to see you yesterday.
Did you have to do it yesterday?
Didn't you have to do it yesterday? / Weren't you supposed to do it yesterday?
I used to be a student.
I was going to call you.
I was going to do it.
We were going to do it.
We were going to do them.

koncept: Imperfect tense of regular verbs (llamar -> llamaba, tener -> tenía)
Expressing obligation in the imperfect (tenía que + infinitive)
Three irregular verbs in the imperfect: ver (veía), ser (era), and ir (iba)
Using iba a + infinitive to express 'was going to do something'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the preposition 'por' and contrasts it with 'para'. The teacher explains how 'por' carries the meaning of 'because of' or indicates a duration of time, using examples such as 'por esta razón' and 'por tres días'. The student also practices building future and conditional forms with 'quedarse'.

fraser.es: Por esta razón no quiero ir.
fraser.en: Because of this reason I don't want to go.
I'm buying it because of you.
I will stay for three days.

fraser.es: Me quedaría por tres días, pero tengo que trabajar.
fraser.en: I would stay for three days, but I have to work.

koncept: Distinction between para (recipient/destination) and por (cause/reason/duration)
Por in the sense of 'because of' (por qué, porque, por esta razón)
Por for duration of time (por tres días)
Masculine gender of 'el día' despite ending in -a
Review of future tense (-ré) and conditional tense (-ría) with quedar(se)

lektioner.om: This lesson explores additional uses of 'por', specifically for expressing cause ('because of') and exchanges ('in exchange for'). It highlights the crucial grammatical rule that infinitives follow prepositions rather than -ing forms. The instructor also introduces common false friends like 'discutir' and 'actual', contrasting them with their true English equivalents.

ord.en: to argue / to have an argument / to discuss

fraser.en: I have come because of you.

fraser.es: Es por ti que hemos venido.
fraser.en: It is because of you that we have come.
I would change this one for that one.
I would change these ones for those ones.
I would change these ones for those ones. (feminine)
Would you change these ones for those ones?

fraser.es: ¿Por qué no cambiarías estas por esas?
fraser.en: Why wouldn't you change these ones for those ones?
It is a way of doing it.

fraser.es: No creo en discutir de esta forma.
fraser.en: I don't believe in arguing in this way.

koncept: Using 'por' for causes ('because of') and exchanges/substitutions
Using the infinitive (to form) instead of the gerund (-ing) after prepositions (por, de, en, para)
False friends in Spanish: 'discutir' (to argue) and 'actual' (current)
Imperfect past of -ar verbs using the '-aba' ending with 'estar' (estaba, estábamos)
Overlapping present tense forms between 'creer' (creo) and 'crear' (creo)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how 'para' is required when an English infinitive expresses purpose ('in order to'). It reviews ongoing past and present actions with estar + gerund versus the imperfect tense. Finally, it introduces adjective derivation from verbs using the suffixes '-ante' and '-ente', and explores how Spanish weekdays derive from planetary names.

fraser.en: We have spoken in order to resolve it.
We have spoken in order to try to resolve it.
I am here to see you.
I have called you in order to speak about it.

fraser.es: Estoy tomando un curso de español.
fraser.en: I am taking a Spanish course.

fraser.es: Estaba tomando un curso de español.
fraser.en: I was taking a Spanish course.
I was taking a Spanish course.

koncept: Using 'para' before an infinitive when 'to' expresses purpose ('in order to')
Continuous actions with estar + gerund (-ando/-iendo) vs. the imperfect tense (-aba/-ía)
Using the infinitive instead of -ing for activities as subjects (e.g., 'Bailar es saludable')
Forming adjectives from verbs with -ante (-ar verbs) and -ente (-er/-ir verbs)
Etymology of Spanish days of the week connected to celestial bodies/planets

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how to express 'could' in the past using the imperfect tense ('podía') and contrasts it with the conditional ('podría'). It introduces the pluperfect tense ('había' + participle) for expressing 'had done', along with the adverb 'ya' (already) and 'buscar' (to look for). It also covers the conditional perfect ('habría' + participle) for 'would have done'.

ord.en: to look for / to search for

fraser.es: No podía hacerlo porque no tenía el tiempo.
fraser.en: I couldn't do it because I didn't have the time.

fraser.es: Él quería cenar conmigo, pero yo ya había cenado.
fraser.en: He wanted to dine with me, but I had dined already.

fraser.es: Él lo buscaba porque yo lo había perdido.
fraser.en: He was looking for it because I had lost it.

koncept: Distinction between past could (podía) and conditional could (podría)
Imperfect past (line past) with -aba / -ía endings
Pluperfect tense formed with imperfect of haber (había) + past participle (-ado / -ido)
Conditional perfect formed with habría + past participle
Placement and usage of 'ya' (already)
Reflexive usage with conditional perfect (me habría perdido)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how past participles (-ado/-ido) formed from verbs can also function as adjectives that agree in gender and number with nouns. It clarifies that these participle-adjectives typically pair with 'estar' when describing a state, but 'ser' is required when identifying or classifying the subject as a noun phrase (e.g., 'es una persona cerrada', 'es una silla mojada').

fraser.en: I would like to have gone.
I get tired / I tire myself.
I have gotten tired / I have tired myself.
He is closed to the idea.

koncept: Past participles (-ado/-ido) used as adjectives
Agreement in gender and number when past participles function as adjectives
Using estar with past-participle adjectives expressing a state
Using ser when categorizing or defining a noun ('es una persona...', 'es una silla...'), even with temporary adjectives

lektioner.om: The lesson introduces compound structures like 'should have' (debería haber...) and 'could have' (podría haber...) followed by past participles. It covers key irregular past participles (roto, muerto, abierto, dicho, hecho) and explains how they function both in perfect tenses and as adjectives with estar. The lesson finishes with an insightful historical linguistics note on the Latin 'f' to Spanish silent 'h' consonant shift to help students recognize vocabulary cognates.

ord.en: said / told (past participle of decir); a saying (noun)
done / made (past participle of hacer); a fact (noun)

fraser.en: it is canceled (referring to a feminine noun, e.g., la fiesta)

fraser.es: lo debería haber cancelado / debería haberlo cancelado

fraser.en: I have done it / made it

fraser.es: debería haberlo hecho / lo debería haber hecho

koncept: Compound conditional structures: 'debería haber...' (should have...) and 'podría haber...' (could have...)
Past participles functioning as adjectives with estar (and ser where applicable)
Irregular past participles: romper -> roto, morir -> muerto, abrir -> abierto, decir -> dicho, hacer -> hecho
Historical phonetic shifts between Latin/English 'F' and Spanish silent 'H' (and 'W' vs 'G/GU')

lektioner.om: In this lesson, the instructor explains that Spanish prepositions must precede relative and interrogative pronouns rather than stranding at the end of a sentence like in English. Students practice connecting relative clauses using 'con que', 'con quien', and 'con cuál', as well as forming questions with 'quién' and its plural form 'quiénes'. The lesson also touches on deducing infinitive forms from past participles (unidos -> unir) and reviews the imperfect form 'iba'.

fraser.en: We are going to the United States.

fraser.es: Es la chica con que trabajaba.
fraser.en: It's the girl I was working with.

fraser.es: La chica con que iba a la fiesta.
fraser.en: The girl I was going to the party with.
I don't know which one he wants.
I don't know which one he wants to see.

fraser.es: No sé con cuál quiere hacerlo.
fraser.en: I don't know which one he wants to do it with.
Who is here? / Who is it?

fraser.es: No sé con quién tengo que hacerlo.
fraser.en: I don't know who I have to do it with.

fraser.es: No sé para quién tengo que hacerlo.
fraser.en: I don't know who I have to do it for.

fraser.es: No sé por quién tengo que hacerlo.
fraser.en: I don't know who I have to do it because of.

koncept: preposition placement (never sentence-final in Spanish)
relative clauses with prepositions (con que, con quien, con cual, con la que)
question words cuál, quién, quiénes
working backwards from participles/adjectives to infinitives (unidos -> unir)
imperfect of ir (iba)
estar for location and omission of aquí

lektioner.om: This lesson highlights the only difference between -er and -ir verbs in Spanish: the 'we' (nosotros) present tense ending (-emos vs. -imos). It also introduces powerful abstract uses of 'lo' combined with adjectives ('lo fácil', 'lo interesante') to express 'the [x] thing', and 'lo de' to mean 'the matter/thing concerning...'. Additionally, 'así' is taught as a natural shorthand for 'like this' or 'like that'.

ord.en: like this / like that / in this way

fraser.es: Lo interesante es que viven aquí.
fraser.en: The interesting thing is that they live here.

fraser.es: Lo interesante es que viven juntos.
fraser.en: The interesting thing is that they live together.

fraser.es: Lo fácil es que vienen juntos.
fraser.en: The easy thing is that they come together.

fraser.es: Lo complicado es que vienen juntos.
fraser.en: The complicated thing is that they come together.

fraser.es: No quiero hablar de lo de Juan así.
fraser.en: I don't want to speak about Juan's business like this.
I want to organize that thing tomorrow / the thing about tomorrow.
But I don't want to organize it like this.

koncept: The distinction between -er (-emos) and -ir (-imos) verbs in the present 'we' (nosotros) form
Using 'lo + adjective' to mean 'the [adjective] thing' (e.g., lo interesante, lo fácil, lo complicado)
Using 'lo de + noun/person' to mean 'the thing about / that business about' (e.g., lo de Juan, lo de mañana)
Adverbial use of 'así' meaning 'like this / like that'

lektioner.om: Introduces the 'point in the past' (preterite tense) for -ar verbs, teaching the -é ending for 'yo' and the accented -ó ending for 'él/ella/usted'. Highlights the importance of stress differentiation between present 'hablo' and preterite 'habló'. Practiced verbs include hablar, comprar, enviar, and olvidar, alongside time expressions like todavía and ayer.

fraser.en: I didn't send it to you.
I didn't send it to you yet.

fraser.es: No sé por qué no habló conmigo.
fraser.en: I don't know why he didn't speak with me.

fraser.es: Lo iba a hacer, pero lo olvidé.
fraser.en: I was going to do it, but I forgot it.

koncept: Preterite tense for regular -ar verbs (-é for 'yo', -ó for 'él/ella/usted')
Contrast between present tense 'hablo' (stress on stem) and preterite 'habló' (stress on ending)
Passive reflexive construction in the past (se envió = it was sent)
Combining the imperfect ('iba a...') with preterite ('lo olvidé')

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the preterite past tense endings for -er/-ir verbs (-í and -ió) using verbs like comer, salir, and ver. It explores comparisons with 'más que' emphasizing the use of subject pronouns (yo, él) to avoid negative language transfer from English. It also covers double negation with 'nada' and 'nadie', time expressions with 'durar' and 'durante', and word derivations connected to 'par' and 'parar'.

fraser.es: No sé por qué no salió todavía.
fraser.en: I don't know why she didn't leave yet.

fraser.es: Lo vi pero no me vio.
fraser.en: I saw him, but he didn't see me.
He ate for/during half an hour.
He spoke for/during half an hour.

fraser.es: Habló durante media hora sin parar.
fraser.en: He spoke for half an hour without stopping.

koncept: Past tense (preterite) for -er/-ir verbs: -í (I) and -ió (he/she/it/you formal)
Comparison using 'más que' with subject pronouns (más que yo, más que él)
Avoidance of English negative transfer with pronouns (using yo/él instead of me/him after 'than')
Double negatives in Spanish (no vi nada, nadie vio nada)
Use of infinitive after prepositions (sin parar)
Etymological connections of 'par' (parar, comparar, preparar, reparar, separar)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the preterite 'nosotros' (we) forms across -ar, -er, and -ir verbs. It highlights that -ar and -ir verbs share the exact same 'nosotros' endings in both present and past tenses (-amos and -imos), relying on context for clarification, whereas -er verbs change from present -emos to past -imos.

fraser.en: When we speak, I understand everything.
When we spoke, I understood everything.

fraser.es: Nos perdemos siempre, pero no nos perdimos ayer.
fraser.en: We always get lost, but we didn't get lost yesterday.

fraser.es: No salimos a menudo, pero salimos ayer.
fraser.en: We don't go out often, but we went out yesterday.

koncept: Preterite tense for 'nosotros' forms: -amos for -ar verbs, -imos for -er and -ir verbs
Identical present and preterite forms for 'nosotros' in -ar (-amos) and -ir (-imos) verbs
Distinction between present (-emos) and preterite (-imos) in 'nosotros' for -er verbs
Using context or time markers (ayer, mañana) to resolve tense ambiguity in 'nosotros' forms

lektioner.om: This lesson explores how the imperfect ('line in the past') and preterite ('dot/point in the past') interact within the same sentence, such as an ongoing background action interrupted by a single completed event. It demonstrates these concepts with verbs like cocinar, sonar, hablar, and llegar, and applies both past perspectives to stative/perception verbs like gustar and parecer.

fraser.en: I was cooking when the phone rang.
I was cooking when the phone rang.

fraser.es: Hablaba por teléfono cuando María llegó.
fraser.en: I was speaking on the phone when María arrived.
I didn't like it (ongoing/was not pleasing me).
It seemed good to me (point in time).
It seemed / was seeming good to me (line in time).

fraser.es: Me parecía bien, pero cuando lo vi no me gustó.
fraser.en: It seemed good to me, but when I saw it I didn't like it.

koncept: Interplay between imperfect (line in time) and preterite (point in time)
Using 'por teléfono' for 'on/by the phone'
Preterite and imperfect forms of gustar and parecer with indirect object pronouns
Reflexive verb quedar(se) in the past tense

lektioner.om: Explains the preterite of 'dar', noting that despite being an -ar verb it takes -er/-ir past tense endings (di, dio, dimos). Introduces the phonetic rule where indirect object pronouns 'le' and 'les' convert to 'se' when placed before direct object pronouns beginning with 'l' (se lo, se las, etc.). Explains how to resolve the resulting ambiguity by adding prepositional clarification tags with 'a' ('a él', 'a ella', 'a ustedes') while maintaining pronoun reduplication.

fraser.en: he didn't give it to us
I gave it to him / her / them / you guys
he sent it to you guys

fraser.es: no se lo envió a ustedes todavía
fraser.en: he didn't send it to you guys yet

fraser.es: no sé si se lo envié
fraser.en: I don't know if I sent it to him

koncept: past tense of dar (irregular -ar verb adopting -er/-ir endings: di, dio, dimos)
double object pronoun phonetic transformation (le/les + lo/la/los/las -> se lo/la/los/las)
clarification and emphasis using prepositional phrases with 'a' (e.g., 'a él', 'a ella', 'a ustedes') with pronoun reduplication
contrast between reduplicated 'a' phrases and non-reduplicated prepositional phrases with 'para'

lektioner.om: Introduces the reflexive verb acordarse with its stem-changing O->UE pattern in the present tense. Reviews indirect object pronoun combinations with double object pronouns (se lo di). Explains the essential role of the preposition 'a' when clarifying the receiver/experiencer with gustar, highlighting how omitting 'a' changes the meaning entirely.

fraser.es: No me acuerdo si se lo di a él o a ella.
fraser.en: I don't remember if I gave it to him or to her.

fraser.es: No nos acordamos si se lo dimos a él o a ellas.
fraser.en: We don't remember if we gave it to him or to them.
She likes it. (It is pleasing to her.)
She liked it. (It was pleasing to her.)

koncept: Reflexive verbs with boot/stem change (acordarse -> me acuerdo vs no nos acordamos)
Clarification using preposition 'a' with indirect object pronouns (a él, a ella, a ellas)
Using gustar with clarification ('a ella le gusta' vs 'ella le gusta')
Past tense (preterite) of gustar (gustó)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the remaining forms of the preterite tense (the point in the past): the informal 'tú' form (-aste / -iste) and the 'ellos/ustedes' form (-aron / -ieron). It also explains how to express time in the past using 'hace' (e.g., 'hace dos semanas' for 'two weeks ago') and introduces 'anoche' (last night). Finally, the teacher guides a comprehensive review comparing the full preterite conjugations of -ar and -er/-ir verbs.

fraser.en: I saw him two weeks ago.
I responded to her seven weeks ago.

fraser.es: Se lo respondí hace un mes.
fraser.en: I responded to her it one month ago.
Did you go out last night?
Didn't you go out last night?
Why didn't you wait for me?

koncept: Using 'hace' for time ago (e.g. hace dos semanas, hace un mes)
Double object pronouns with 'le' becoming 'se' (se lo respondí)
Preterite tense endings for 'tú' (-aste / -iste)
Preterite tense endings for 'ellos / ellas / ustedes' (-aron / -ieron)
Contrast between line in the past (imperfect) and point in the past (preterite)
Full preterite paradigm summary for -ar and -er/-ir verbs

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces 'más' used as 'else' with words like 'nada' and 'nadie', alongside the noun 'vez' to indicate occasions (once, again, one more time, at the same time). It expands on possessive adjectives ('mi', 'tu', 'nuestro', 'su') and the word 'propio' ('own'), emphasizing that possessive markers agree in gender and number with the possessed noun, not the possessor. Key past tense forms for both regular and irregular verbs are practiced in varied communicative contexts.

ord.en: at the same time / at a time

fraser.en: Didn't you see me last night?
I want to see them one more time.
I want to see them again.
¿Did you go out to dance again?

fraser.es: Llegó tarde a mi casa otra vez.
fraser.en: He arrived late to my house again.

fraser.es: Llegó a mi casa otra vez queriendo hablar conmigo.
fraser.en: He arrived at my house again wanting to speak with me.

fraser.es: ¿A qué hora llegaron a tu casa?
fraser.en: At what time did they arrive at your house?

fraser.es: Todos llegaron a mi casa a la vez.
fraser.en: Everybody arrived at my house at the same time.

fraser.es: No encontré nada más en tu casa.
fraser.en: I didn't find anything else in your house.
I want to go to his/their house.
I want to go to his/their houses.

fraser.es: Lo vi con mis propios ojos.
fraser.en: I saw it with my own eyes.

fraser.es: Quiero vivir en mi propia casa.
fraser.en: I want to live in my own house.

koncept: Using 'más' to express 'else' ('nada más', 'nadie más', 'una vez más')
The noun 'vez' for instances/occasions ('una vez', 'otra vez', 'a la vez')
Possessive adjectives (mi/mis, tu/tus, nuestro/nuestra/nuestros/nuestras, su/sus) and gender/number agreement with the possessed object
Using 'propio/a/os/as' for 'own'
Past tense conjugation review for -ar and -er/-ir verbs ('comiste', 'vi/viste/vio/vimos/vieron', 'hablé/hablaste/habló/hablamos/hablaron', 'llegaste/llegó/llegaron', 'encontré')

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how Spanish handles possession differently from English. Instead of possessive adjectives with body parts, Spanish uses indirect object pronouns and definite articles (e.g., 'me duele la pierna'). It also covers possessive constructions using 'de' (e.g., 'la casa de José') and introduces 'solo' (only/just).

fraser.es: No me duele la pierna más.
Vamos a la casa de José.
fraser.en: We are going to José's house.

fraser.es: Vamos a la fiesta de María.
fraser.en: We are going to María's party.

fraser.es: No hablé con nadie más en la fiesta de María, solo hablé contigo.
fraser.en: I didn't speak with anybody else at María's party, I only spoke with you.

koncept: expressing possession with 'de' instead of possessive apostrophe 's
using indirect object pronouns with body parts instead of possessive determiners (e.g., 'me duele la pierna')
stem-changing verb 'doler' (o -> ue)
position of 'solo' for emphasis

lektioner.om: The teacher explains Spanish pronunciation, stress, and accentuation rules. Students learn the natural stress positions for words ending in vowels/n/s versus other consonants, and how written accents mark exceptions. The lesson also introduces diacritical accents used to distinguish monosyllabic homonyms and interrogative words.
koncept: Natural stress rules (vowel/n/s -> penultimate syllable; other consonants -> last syllable)
Written accents (tildes) for rule-breaking stress (e.g., -ción words, preterite endings -ó/-ió)
Diacritical accents on homonyms/monosyllables (sí/si, mí/mi, tú/tu, sé/se)
Question words vs relative pronouns (dónde/donde, cómo/como)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces demonstrative adjectives and pronouns in Spanish, explaining masculine, feminine, plural forms, and abstract neuter forms ('esto', 'eso'). It also explores using 'tan' (so) with adjectives and uses imperfect context setting to anchor sentences containing ambiguous past/present -amos/-imos verb forms.

fraser.es: Nada me gusta más que esto.
fraser.en: I don't like anything more than this (Nothing pleases me more than this).

fraser.es: Nada me gustó más que eso.
fraser.en: I didn't like anything more than that (Nothing pleased me more than that).

fraser.es: Estábamos tan cansados que dormimos todo el día.
fraser.en: We were so tired that we slept all day.

fraser.es: Estábamos tan cansados cuando llegamos que dormimos todo el día.
fraser.en: We were so tired when we arrived that we slept all day.

fraser.es: No sé cuántas veces lo visité.
fraser.en: I don't know how many times I visited him.

fraser.es: No sé cuántas veces lo visitaron.
fraser.en: I don't know how many times they visited him.

fraser.es: No sé cuántas veces la visitaron.
fraser.en: I don't know how many times they visited her.

koncept: Demonstrative adjectives (este/esta/estos/estas, ese/esa/esos/esas)
Neuter demonstrative pronouns (esto, eso) for abstract or non-gendered ideas
Using the imperfect tense ('estábamos') to set the continuous background/context for past actions
Expressing quantity and frequency ('tan', 'cuánto/a/os/as', 'cuántas veces')

lektioner.om: Introduces the concept and formation of the Spanish subjunctive (referred to as the 'mood tense'). Explains how verb endings swap between -ar and -er/-ir groups, and demonstrates its obligatory use following verbs of wanting like 'querer que'.

fraser.en: I want you to wait for him / for it.
Do you want me to wait for you?
Do you want me to wait for you? (clarified)

koncept: Introduction to the Present Subjunctive (Mood Tense)
Forming the subjunctive by switching verb family endings (-ar verbs take -e/-en/-emos; -er/-ir verbs take -a/-an/-amos)
First-person singular (yo) taking the same form as third-person singular (él/ella/usted) in the subjunctive
Obligatory subjunctive with expressions of wanting/wishing followed by 'que' (e.g., 'Quiero que...')
Translating English 'I want you to [verb]' structures to 'Quiero que [subjunctive]'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces 'lo que' for 'what' when used in statements rather than direct or indirect questions. It expands the subjunctive triggers to include verbs and expressions of necessity and preference ('necesitar que', 'hace falta que', 'preferir que'). It also practices combining indirect and direct object pronouns ('se lo') with the subjunctive, as well as clarifying ambiguous pronouns using 'a él' or 'a ella'.

ord.en: to lack / to be missing / to be short of

fraser.es: No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablamos.
fraser.en: I don't want you to speak about what we spoke about.

fraser.es: No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablábamos.
fraser.en: I don't want you to speak about what we were speaking about.
I need you to prepare it (formal).

fraser.es: Necesito que prepare lo que falta.
fraser.en: I need you to prepare what's missing (formal).
It is necessary that we eat soon.

fraser.es: Prefiero que no se queden aquí.
fraser.en: I prefer them not to stay here.
I prefer you to give it to him/her (informal).

fraser.es: Prefiero que se lo des a él.
fraser.en: I prefer you to give it to him.

fraser.es: Prefiero que se lo des a ella.
fraser.en: I prefer you to give it to her.

koncept: Distinction between interrogative 'qué' and relative pronoun 'lo que'
Subjunctive mood triggers expressing necessity, requirement, and preference (necesitar que, hace falta que, preferir que)
Using the imperfect ('hablábamos') to resolve ambiguity between present and past ('hablamos')
Clarifying the indirect object pronoun 'se' with prepositional phrases ('a él', 'a ella')

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the double meaning of 'contar' (to count / to recount) and its prepositional phrase 'contar con' (to count on). It reviews subjunctive mood triggers with verbs like 'esperar que' and 'me gusta que', and thoroughly explains the grammatical necessity and usage of the personal 'a' in Spanish to distinguish subjects from direct objects due to flexible word order.

ord.en: to count / to recount / to tell

fraser.en: I want you to tell me.
I want you (plural) to tell me something.
I want you to count on me.
I hope that you count on me.
We hope that they count on María.

fraser.es: Esperamos que lo cuenten a María.
fraser.en: We hope that they tell it to María.
I hope that they see María.
I hope that you (informal) understand David.
I hope that you (formal) understand David.
I want him/her to see the man.
I want the man to see.

fraser.es: Me gusta que la profesora visite.
fraser.en: I like that the teacher visits.

fraser.es: Me gusta que visite a la profesora.
fraser.en: I like that he/she visits the teacher.

koncept: The verb 'contar' meaning both 'to count' and 'to recount/tell stories'
Subjunctive/mood tense of stem-changing verb 'contar' (cuente, cuentes, cuenten)
Subjunctive form of 'ver' (vea, vean) formed from 'veo' to avoid confusion with 'va/van'
The personal 'a' used before specific human direct objects to disambiguate flexible Spanish word order
Contraction of 'a + el' into 'al'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces imperative commands in Spanish. It explains how formal, plural, and all negative commands use the switched-vowel mood tense (subjunctive), while affirmative informal commands use a shortcut by dropping the '-s' from the present indicative 'tú' form. It also covers the rule for pronoun placement, attaching pronouns to the end of affirmative commands and placing them before negative commands.

fraser.es: No se lo des a él.

koncept: Imperative / Command forms using the subjunctive/mood tense for formal, plural, and negative informal commands
Positive informal (tú) command shortcut: dropping the -s from the present tense tú form
Pronoun attachment: enclitic object/reflexive pronouns attached to the end of affirmative commands vs. placed before negative commands

lektioner.om: This lesson covers indirect commands using 'que' plus the subjunctive to express 'let him/her/it do something'. It also introduces the rule requiring the subjunctive after 'cuando' when referring to future, unfulfilled events, contrasting it with the indicative used for habitual actions.

fraser.en: let him shut up! / let him be quiet!
when we eat together we speak (generally)
when we eat together we will speak (future)
we see her when we go (generally)
we will see her when we go (future)

koncept: informal positive commands shortcut (dropping -s)
indirect commands using 'que' + subjunctive (third-person commands / wishes)
subjunctive after 'cuando' when referring to future events vs indicative for general habitual actions
irregular subjunctive form of ir (vaya, vayan, vayamos)

lektioner.om: This lesson explores obligatory triggers for the subjunctive mood, specifically 'para que' (so that / in order that). It introduces new stem-changing verbs like 'elegir' (e -> i) and 'volver' (o -> ue), contrasting them with their non-changing 'nosotros' forms. The teacher also explains the etymology and use of 'por' vs 'para', reflexive verbs, and the connector 'también'.

ord.en: to meet up / to find oneself / each other
to return / to come back / to go back

fraser.es: No quiero que elijas por mí.
fraser.en: I don't want you to choose for me (on my behalf).
I don't want it to break.
We have met up in order to speak.
We have cooked so that they eat.

fraser.es: Lo he hecho para que vuelvas.
fraser.en: I have done it so that you come back.

fraser.es: Lo he hecho para que vuelvan.
fraser.en: I have done it so that they come back.

fraser.es: Lo han hecho para que volvamos.
fraser.en: They have done it so that we come back.
So that you also come back.

fraser.es: Hemos hecho todo para que tú también vuelvas.
fraser.en: We have done everything so that you also come back.

koncept: E to I stem-changing verbs (elegir -> elijo, eliges)
Por vs Para (on behalf of vs for/intended for)
Subjunctive after 'para que' (so that / in order that)
Reflexive verbs for non-agentive actions (romperse, encontrarse)
Past participle of hacer (hecho)
