O to UE stem-changing verbs (volver -> vuelvo, vuelvas; volvamos in nosotros)

lektioner.om: This lesson demonstrates how using the subjunctive mood transforms words like 'donde', 'como', 'cuando', and 'lo que' into '-ever' indefinite expressions ('wherever', 'however', 'whenever', 'whatever'). It also covers the irregular informal imperative of hacer (haz), stem-changing verbs of the seguir family, and the subjunctive forms of ser (sea) along with the fixed phrase 'sea lo que sea'.

ord.en: to follow / to continue / to carry on
that is / I mean / or rather

fraser.en: I'll follow you wherever you go.
I prefer it to be like this.
Whatever it is / whatever will be, will be.

koncept: Informal imperative shortcut and irregular imperative of hacer (haz)
Using the subjunctive (mood tense) with relative words (donde, como, lo que, cuando) to mean 'wherever', 'however', 'whatever', 'whenever'
E-to-I stem-changing verbs in the present indicative (seguir, conseguir, perseguir, elegir)
Irregular subjunctive of ser (sea)

lektioner.om: The teacher introduces 'hay' and its past form 'había' as impersonal forms of 'haber'. The lesson explores how subjunctive is triggered when inquiring about or referring to hypothetical/unconfirmed entities (using 'que' relative clauses). The teacher also discusses the broader linguistic concept of language 'value systems' reflected in grammatical requirements like the subjunctive.

fraser.es: Hay alguien aquí que quiere hablar con usted.
fraser.en: There is somebody here that wants to speak with you.
Is there somebody here that speaks Spanish?

fraser.es: Hay dos personas aquí que hablan español.
fraser.en: There are two people here that speak Spanish.

fraser.es: Había dos personas aquí que hablaban español.
fraser.en: There were two people here that spoke Spanish.

fraser.es: Tiene que haber algo que puedas hacer.
fraser.en: There has to be something that you can do.

koncept: Use of 'hay' (present) and 'había' (imperfect) derived from 'haber'
Invariable nature of 'hay' and 'había' (never pluralized to *habían in standard existential usage)
Subjunctive after existential questions or indefinite/unconfirmed antecedents (¿Hay alguien aquí que hable...?, Tiene que haber algo que puedas...)
Imperfect vs Preterite with background states/abilities ('hablaban español')

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the subjunctive mood following impersonal expressions composed of 'es + adjective + que' (such as 'es terrible que', 'es posible que', 'es necesario que', and 'es importante que'). The instructor contrasts this with 'si' clauses which take the indicative mood. The lesson also explores colloquial expressions with '¡Qué fuerte!' and the phrase 'no hace falta que'.

ord.en: to answer / to respond / to reply

fraser.en: There should be something to eat.
It is terrible that you eat this.
It is terrible if you eat this.

fraser.es: Es posible que vayamos más tarde.
fraser.en: It is possible that we go later.
How crazy/heavy that he is here!

fraser.es: Está bien que preguntes, pero no es necesario que responda.
fraser.en: It's fine that you ask, but it's not necessary that I respond.
It's not necessary that I respond.

fraser.es: Es importante que lo encontremos pronto.
fraser.en: It is important that we find it soon.

koncept: Subjunctive (mood tense) triggered by impersonal expressions: 'es + [adjective] + que'
Contrast between 'es terrible que' (triggers subjunctive) and 'es terrible si' (indicative)
Exclamatory phrases with subjunctive ('¡Qué fuerte que...!')
Alternative impersonal structure: 'no hace falta que + subjunctive'

lektioner.om: This lesson explores how verbs like seguir, empezar, and terminar interact with infinitives (using prepositions like 'a' or 'de') versus gerunds (-ando/-iendo), highlighting shifts in meaning such as 'finish doing' (terminar de) versus 'end up doing' (terminar + gerund). It reinforces subjunctive triggers with impersonal expressions and future-oriented 'cuando'. The instructor concludes with practical advice on internalizing the subjunctive mood through reading and online chatting.

fraser.en: It's probable that he continues speaking / He will probably keep speaking.

fraser.es: Es imperativo que siga siendo gratis.
fraser.en: It's imperative that it continues being free.

fraser.es: Es espectacular que comiencen a hablar español.
fraser.en: It's spectacular that they start to speak Spanish.

fraser.es: Es espectacular que comiencen hablando español.
fraser.en: It's spectacular that they start out speaking Spanish.

fraser.es: Quiero que hablen conmigo cuando terminen de venderlos.
fraser.en: I want you guys to speak with me when you finish selling them.

fraser.es: Quiero que hablen conmigo cuando terminen vendiéndolos.
fraser.en: I want you guys to speak with me when you end up selling them.

koncept: seguir + gerund (continuing an action)
empezar/comenzar a + infinitive vs. empezar/comenzar + gerund (starting to do vs. starting out doing)
terminar de + infinitive (to finish doing) vs. terminar + gerund (to end up doing)
subjunctive mood triggered by impersonal expressions (es probable que, es imperativo que, es espectacular que)
subjunctive after cuando referring to future/anticipated events

lektioner.om: This lesson reviews and consolidates various triggers for the subjunctive ('mood tense') in Spanish, introducing the verb 'dejar' (to leave a message). The teacher contrasts reported speech ('decir que' + indicative) with indirect commands ('decir que' + subjunctive) and demonstrates subjunctive triggers such as 'cuando' referring to the future, impersonal expressions like 'es esencial que', and 'ojalá'. Cultural context on the Arabic origins of 'ojalá' and tips on noticing nuances/tones expressed through the subjunctive are also discussed.

fraser.es: Quiero que me dejes un mensaje.
fraser.en: I want you to leave me a message. (informal)

fraser.es: Quiero decirle que me deje un mensaje.
fraser.en: I want to tell him to leave me a message.

fraser.es: Cuando te deje el mensaje, llámame.
fraser.en: When he leaves you the message, call me. (informal)

fraser.es: Es esencial que vea mi mensaje.
fraser.en: It is essential that he/she sees my message.

koncept: Subjunctive mood triggers review (commands, wanting/telling someone to do something, future with 'cuando', impersonal expressions, 'ojalá')
Imperative pronoun placement (attached at the end of positive commands: déjeme, llámame)
Indirect requests using 'decir que' + subjunctive vs. reported speech with indicative
Subjunctive after 'ojalá' to express hopes/wishes
Subjunctive conjugation of 'ver' (vea) and 'ser' (sea)
Cognate patterns (-tial to -cial: esencial, espacial)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the accidental or unintentional 'se' structure in Spanish (using 'se' combined with indirect object pronouns 'me', 'te', 'le', 'nos', 'les' to express that an event happened unexpectedly to someone, equivalent to the English idiom 'it happened on me'). The teacher reviews previous uses of 'se' before practicing this structure with verbs such as cerrar, quemar, and acabar.

fraser.en: The dinner is burning on me.

fraser.es: La batería siempre se me acaba.
fraser.en: The battery always runs out on me.
Does the battery run out on you? (informal)
Does the battery run out on you? (formal)
Does the battery run out on you (plural)?

koncept: accidental/involuntary 'se' constructions (se + indirect object pronoun: se me, se te, se le, se nos, se les)
review of multiple uses of 'se' (reflexive, phonetic substitute for 'le/les', and accidental aspect)
past tense (preterite) with involuntary 'se'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the Spanish past subjunctive (past mood tense). The teacher demonstrates how to construct it by taking the 3rd-person plural preterite ('they' point in the past, e.g., hablaron, comieron), changing the final 'on' to 'an' (hablaran, comieran), and deriving all other subject forms from there. The lesson also covers using 'volver a' for repeating actions and shows how past triggers like 'quería que' and 'para que' require the past subjunctive.

fraser.es: No quiero que la puerta se me cierre otra vez.
fraser.en: I don't want the door to close on me again.

fraser.es: No quiero que la puerta vuelva a cerrarse.
fraser.en: I don't want the door to close again.

fraser.es: No quiero que vuelva a pasar.
fraser.en: I don't want it to happen again.
I wanted them to eat with us.
I was hoping that he would call me.
We needed to speak with him.
We needed him to speak with us.
I called you again in order to organize.

fraser.es: Volví a llamarte para que organizáramos.
fraser.en: I called you again so that we would organize.

koncept: The construction 'volver a + infinitive' meaning to do something again
Formation of the imperfect subjunctive (past mood tense) from the 3rd person plural preterite ('they' form)
Conjugation of the past subjunctive endings (-ara/-iera, -aras/-ieras, -áramos/-iéramos, -aran/-ieran)
Triggering past subjunctive with past wishing/hoping/requiring verbs (quería que, esperaba que, necesitábamos que, para que)
Using infinitives with prepositions ('para + infinitive') to simplify or avoid subjunctive structures when subjects align

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how impersonal evaluations with 'ser' + adjective + 'que' trigger the subjunctive (both present and imperfect). It also introduces a strategy to bypass the subjunctive by rephrasing statements with the neuter 'lo' + adjective + 'es que' followed by the indicative.

fraser.es: No es muy relevante que lo encontraran.
fraser.en: It's not very relevant that they found it.

fraser.es: No es muy relevante que lo encuentren.
fraser.en: It's not very relevant that they find it.

fraser.es: Era muy relevante que lo encontraran.
fraser.en: It was very relevant that they found it.
It's incredible that they come back.
The incredible thing is that they come back.

fraser.es: Lo increíble es que vuelven a hacerlo.
fraser.en: The incredible thing is that they do it again.

fraser.es: Es increíble que vuelvan a hacerlo.
fraser.en: It is incredible that they do it again.

fraser.es: Es increíble que volvieran a hacerlo.
fraser.en: It's incredible that they did it again.

koncept: Subjunctive trigger with impersonal expressions: ser/estar + adjective + que
Imperfect of ser: era
Present subjunctive vs. imperfect subjunctive based on time frame
Neuter article 'lo' + adjective to mean 'the [adjective] thing'
Avoiding the subjunctive using 'lo [adjective] es que + indicative'

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces hypothetical conditional sentences using the past subjunctive (imperfect subjunctive) after 'si' combined with the conditional tense in the main clause. It also covers past hypothetical constructions ('If you had told me... I would have gone') using the pluperfect subjunctive and conditional perfect. Finally, the instructor explains the alternative '-se' endings of the imperfect subjunctive and notes that they are interchangeable in meaning with the '-ra' endings.

fraser.es: Que lo compraras no es mi problema.
fraser.en: That you bought it is not my problem.

fraser.es: Que le contaras no es mi problema.
fraser.en: That you told him is not my problem.
If I could cook, I would cook.
If I could cancel it, I would cancel it.

fraser.es: Si me lo hubieras contado, habría ido.
fraser.en: If you had told me, I would have gone.
If we had known, we would have gone.
If you saw it, you would understand it.
If you saw it, you would understand it.

koncept: Past subjunctive with hypothetical 'si' (if) clauses
Past subjunctive in noun clauses introduced by 'que'
Conditional tense paired with past subjunctive (second and third conditionals)
Pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle) and conditional perfect (habría + participle)
Alternative past subjunctive endings (-se forms: hablase, entendiese)

lektioner.om: This lesson synthesizes the broad overview of Spanish tenses and moods before focusing on irregular verbs. The teacher groups verbs with an '-o' to '-go' irregularity in the first-person singular present (e.g., tener, venir, traer, oír) and explains how this irregularity carries over into the subjunctive (mood tense), shifting systematically from '-go' to '-ga' across all persons.

fraser.en: Tell me. (used answering the phone in Spain)
I want you to bring it.
I don't want you to distract me.

koncept: Irregular '-go' verbs in the present indicative (tengo, vengo, salgo, pongo, digo, hago, oigo, traigo)
Derivatives of traer ending in '-traer' (extraer, atraer, contraer, distraer)
Subjunctive/mood tense formation for '-go' verbs shifting to '-ga', '-gas', etc. (tenga, vengas, traigas, distraigas)
Imperatives derived from the subjunctive (venga, dígame)

lektioner.om: This lesson explains how '-go' verbs behave in the subjunctive mood and in imperative forms. It introduces the shortcut for informal positive commands with '-go' verbs, where dropping '-go' produces the command form (e.g., ten, ven, sal, di). It also contrasts informal vs. formal phone greetings (dime vs. dígame) and practices using the subjunctive after 'cuándo' for future reference.

fraser.en: tell me when you do it (formal)

koncept: -go verbs subjunctive forms ending in -ga/-gas/-gan
Formal imperative vs informal imperative of -go verbs
Shortcut for informal positive commands of -go verbs (dropping -go to form ten, ven, sal, di)
Object pronoun placement with positive and negative imperatives
Subjunctive after 'cuándo' when referring to future events

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces irregular stem formations in the future ('will') and conditional ('would') tenses. Verbs that have a '-go' form in the present indicative contract to '-dr-' stems (e.g., tener -> tendré/tendría, salir -> saldré/saldría). Special irregular stems for hacer (har-), decir (dir-), and poder (podr-) are also explored.

ord.en: I will leave / I will go out
I would leave / I would go out
I will do / I will make
I would do / I would make
I will say / I will tell
I would say / I would tell
I could / I would be able to

fraser.es: Vendríamos más tarde, pero no tenemos tiempo.
fraser.en: We would come later, but we don't have time.

fraser.es: Lo haríamos, pero estamos ocupados ahora.
fraser.en: We would do it, but we're busy now.

koncept: Irregular future and conditional stems for -go verbs (tener -> tendr-, venir -> vendr-, poner -> pondr-, salir -> saldr-)
Highly irregular stems for hacer (har-) and decir (dir-) in the future and conditional
Vowel-drop irregular stem for poder (podr-)
Distinction between podría (I/he/she could) and pondría (I/he/she would put)

lektioner.om: This lesson introduces the pattern of irregular preterite verbs by first reviewing imperfect and regular preterite endings. It explains that irregular preterite stems (such as tuv-, estuv-, and dij-) take a unique hybrid set of unaccented endings (-e and -o from -ar, the rest from -er/-ir). The instructor also notes how speakers can temporarily fall back on the imperfect when speaking quickly.

fraser.en: Where were you guys? / Where were they? (preterite)

koncept: Review of imperfect (line in the past) for ser (era), ir (iba), and ver (veía)
Review of regular preterite (point in the past) endings for -ar and -er/-ir verbs
Irregular preterite stem changes: tener -> tuv-, estar -> estuv-, decir -> dij-
Irregular preterite endings pattern (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron/-eron) with no written accents
Pragmatic use of imperfect vs. preterite when irregular preterite forms are hard to recall

lektioner.om: This lesson explores common irregular preterite stems (such as poner, hacer, venir, traer, and the shared preterite of ser/ir). It demonstrates how to form the past subjunctive (imperfect subjunctive) using the third-person plural preterite stem, highlighting why starting from the 'ellos' form accounts for irregularities like the dropped 'i' in endings like -eron.

fraser.es: Si fuera tú, ... / Si yo fuera tú, ...
Si lo tuviera, te lo contaría.
fraser.en: If I had it, I would tell you (it).
I wanted them to do it.
I wanted us to do it.

koncept: Irregular preterite stem changes (poner -> pus-, hacer -> hic-/hiz-, venir -> vin-, traer -> traj-)
Shared preterite conjugation of ser and ir (fui, fue, fuimos, fuiste, fueron)
Dropping of the 'i' in -ieron for j-stems and fueron (trajeron, dijeron, fueron)
Forming the imperfect subjunctive (past mood tense) from the 3rd person plural preterite (ellos form)

lektioner.om: This lesson trains the student to become an independent language analyst by deducing grammatical rules from examples rather than relying on rote memorization. The teacher guides the student to uncover three specific patterns: why 'demasiado' changes before nouns but remains invariant before adjectives, why certain feminine nouns take 'el' (two syllables starting/ending with 'a'), and how 'uno', 'alguno', and 'ninguno' drop their final '-o' before masculine singular nouns.

fraser.en: I have four too many / I have four extra.
I want a car / one car

koncept: Deducing and formulating grammar rules through analytical observation
Demasiado as an adjective (inflecting for gender/number before nouns) vs. adverb (invariable before adjectives)
Use of the masculine definite article 'el' before two-syllable feminine nouns beginning and ending with 'a' (el agua, el ala, el aula)
Apocope of uno, alguno, and ninguno to un, algún, and ningún before masculine singular nouns

lektioner.om: In this final concluding track, the instructor reviews major regional variations in Spanish, including leísmo, vosotros, voseo, and phonetic features like aspirated S. He provides guidance on continuing language acquisition through media immersion and analytical deconstruction of spoken Spanish, and delivers closing remarks on the Language Transfer project.

ord.en: you (informal singular pronoun in parts of Latin America)

fraser.es: Y solo tenemos que practicar, hablar, y analizar para perfeccionar nuestro español.
fraser.en: And we only have to practice, speak, and analyze to perfect our Spanish.
I see him / her / you formal (leísmo in Spain).

koncept: Dialectal variations (leísmo in Spain vs. direct object pronouns lo/la)
Regional pronouns (vosotros in Spain, voseo in Rioplatense and Latin America)
Phonological differences (aspirated S)
Voseo verb conjugations (podés, querés)
Post-course learning strategies: deconstructing input, listening practice, and exposure
